summary: Offers guidance on how to use the multiplexing features of RTP to support multiple media streams, a design question that has caused much discussion. It explains the options and trade-offs, since RTP's flexibility can complicate application design. It is informational.

eli5.summary: There are many ways to pack several video and audio streams into a call. This document is advice on picking the best way, listing the pros and cons of each.

subtitle: Guidance on RTP multiplexing options for combining multiple media streams

tldr.problem: RTP is flexible and can support multiple media streams (video and audio, multiple cameras, layered encoding, retransmissions) but designers need to choose between using multiple RTP sessions or multiple streams in one session, each with different implications.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8872 examines the multiplexing points in RTP (sessions, SSRCs, payload types), explains the trade-offs for interworking, network QoS, NAT traversal, multicast, and security, then provides guidelines for choosing the best approach for different scenarios.
tldr.outcome: These guidelines help implementers make informed multiplexing choices, improving interoperability and avoiding design mistakes that could cause issues with legacy endpoints or middleboxes.

today: RFC 8872 is an Informational document published in January 2021 and provides the primary guidance for RTP application designers deciding how to structure multiple media streams. It is actively used by WebRTC implementations, video conferencing systems, and any real-time communication application that needs to handle multiple concurrent media streams.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The RTP (Real-time Transport Protocol) is widely used for multimedia communication and was designed from the beginning to support multiple participants and flexible topologies. One of its key features is flexibility in how to represent multiple media streams. For example, an endpoint might have multiple cameras, or a single video stream might be encoded in multiple layers, or a protocol might need a separate retransmission stream to recover lost packets. The challenge is deciding how to structure these streams using RTP's multiplexing points.

RFC 8872 clarifies how to use RTP's multiplexing features to support multiple media streams. The document discusses available options, design trade-offs, and provides guidelines for different use cases. Understanding these choices is important because the wrong multiplexing structure can cause interoperability problems with other applications, complications with network-level mechanisms like QoS, or security issues. The goal is to help application designers make informed decisions that suit their specific needs.
sections.eli5: RTP is very flexible, which is good, but it makes designing a video call app complicated. How do you send multiple video streams? Do you use one connection for everything or separate connections for video and audio? This document answers those questions for different situations.

sections.title: RTP Multiplexing Points and Options
sections.content:
RTP has several multiplexing points where you can distinguish and separate streams. The RTP Session is the highest-level concept—it represents a group of endpoints sharing a common SSRC space and is typically identified by transport-level addresses and ports. An endpoint can have one or more RTP sessions.

The SSRC (Synchronization Source) identifies a single source of an RTP stream within a session. An endpoint can have multiple SSRCs if it sends multiple streams (e.g., video from two cameras). The SSRC identifies a single timing and sequence number space, so different streams must use different SSRCs. The RTP Payload Type identifies the format (codec) of the data and is selected during decoding but is not a true multiplexing point because multiple payload types would require different timing spaces. CSRCs (Contributing Sources) are used by mixers and translators to indicate which sources contributed to the output, but are not a multiplexing point for endpoint streams.

The fundamental design choice is: for multiple media flows, should each use a different RTP session, or should multiple flows share one RTP session (distinguished by different SSRCs)? RFC 8872 explains that there is no single best answer—the choice depends on the application's topology, interworking needs, network environment, and security requirements.
sections.eli5: RTP has a few places you can split things up: sessions (like separate connections), stream IDs (SSRCs), and codec types. Each choice has different effects on whether old phones work, how network routers treat the streams, and whether things are secure.

sections.title: Design Considerations and Trade-offs
sections.content:
For application interworking, when two different RTP applications need to communicate (e.g., a video conferencing system bridging with a broadcast application), the gateway between them must handle potential mismatches in multiplexing choices. If one application uses multiple SSRCs in a session and the other expects a single stream per session, the gateway must adapt, which can complicate implementation and create interoperability risks. Legacy applications that predate the RTP multiplexing guidelines may not handle multiple streams properly, requiring gateways to deliver only a single stream of each media type.

For network considerations, QoS mechanisms work differently with different multiplexing choices. Flow-based QoS (like RSVP) treats all streams in the same 5-tuple (source/destination address and port) identically, so multiple SSRCs in one session get the same QoS treatment. Packet-marking schemes (like Diffserv) can assign different markings to different packets within a transport flow, but must be careful about packet reordering. Multiple RTP sessions require multiple transport flows, which impacts NAT/firewall traversal—each additional transport flow requires additional NAT state and ICE connectivity checks, adding setup time and complexity. For multicast applications, multiple RTP sessions allow receivers to selectively join only the layers or streams they need, improving efficiency for heterogeneous receiver conditions.
sections.eli5: If you use separate connections for each stream, network routers and firewalls have more to track. If you pack everything into one connection, old devices might break. Security gets complicated with multiple streams, especially in group calls. The right choice depends on what matters most for your app: compatibility, network efficiency, or something else.

sections.title: Security and Binding Related Streams
sections.content:
Security considerations arise when using SRTP (Secure RTP). SRTP derives separate keys for each SSRC from a master key, but in multi-party sessions, all parties with a shared key can theoretically send using that key, so sender authentication requires additional mechanisms. When a participant leaves a session, ensuring they can no longer access streams requires rekeying without telling the excluded party—a problem that exists regardless of multiplexing choice but becomes more complex with more streams and participants.

When multiple RTP streams need to be associated together (e.g., a video stream and its retransmission stream, or different layers of a scalable encoding), they must be bound. Binding solutions include RTP/RTCP-based methods (using the CNAME SDES item to relate streams from the same endpoint), SDP signaling-based grouping, and newer mechanisms like the RTP Stream ID (RID) extension that explicitly map media streams. The RID mechanism is preferred because it works consistently whether streams use the same session or separate sessions, making it agnostic of the multiplexing choice. For FEC (Forward Error Correction) streams that protect other streams, multiple RTP sessions allow receivers that cannot use FEC to ignore it at the transport level without processing RTP data.
sections.eli5: When you have multiple video streams (main camera and screen share), the receiver needs to know they're related. You can use stream IDs, connection info, or the sender's name (CNAME) to say 'these go together.' With encryption, you also need to keep track of different keys for different streams and decide who can access what.

sections.title: Guidelines and Recommendations
sections.content:
RFC 8872 recommends using unique SSRCs for different media streams within an RTP session—a fundamental principle that RFC 3550 established and RFC 8860 confirms. Each stream needs its own timing and sequence number space, making separate SSRCs essential. For most point-to-point applications, a single RTP session is simpler than multiple sessions. Multiple RTP sessions are valuable when different streams have genuinely different properties (e.g., scalable layers in multicast where receivers selectively join different groups) or when interworking with applications that require session separation.

For applications sending multiple media types (audio and video), both single-session and multiple-session approaches are viable, and RFC 8860 updates RFC 3550 to support mixed-media sessions. The choice depends on application and network needs: single-session simplifies processing if all media goes over the same transport path, while separate sessions allow independent QoS or different network paths if needed. When designing an application, implementers should consider legacy compatibility (do peers support the chosen model?), whether QoS differentiation is needed, NAT/firewall implications, multicast scalability, and security requirements. Using explicit binding mechanisms like RID makes the application more robust across different multiplexing topologies.
sections.eli5: Basic rule: each stream gets its own ID. For simple calls, put everything in one connection. For fancy setups with layers that some receivers don't need, use separate connections. And always document which streams go together so old apps don't get confused.
